title: Use of brackets and extraction of common factors
summary: Expand brackets and reverse the process by extracting the greatest common numerical and variable factor from every term.
objectives: Expand a factor across every term and track signs accurately.
Identify and extract the greatest common factor of coefficients and variable parts.
Verify complete factorisation by re-expanding and checking that no common factor remains inside.

blocks.text: Expansion multiplies an outside factor into every bracket term. Factorisation reverses that process: identify a factor shared by every term, write it outside a bracket, and divide each original term by it to obtain the bracket contents. The equality must preserve both coefficients and signs.

The greatest common factor gives a complete single-factor extraction. For the numerical part, use the greatest common divisor of the coefficients. For each variable, use the lowest exponent that appears in every term. A variable missing from one term is not common to all terms.

sections.title: Worked example: extract a common factor

content.text: The greatest common numerical factor is 7 and both terms contain a.
Place the common factor outside the bracket.

sections.verification_note: Expanding 7a(2b + 3) gives 14ab + 21a, and 2b and 3 have no further common factor.

blocks.text: Consider coefficients and variables separately. For 18x³y and 24x²y², the greatest numerical factor is 6. The lowest shared power of x is x² and the lowest shared power of y is y. Therefore the greatest common factor is 6x²y.

A negative common factor may be useful when the leading term is negative, because it leaves a positive first term inside the bracket. Either sign can produce an equivalent factorisation, but the chosen factor must divide every term and the re-expanded signs must match exactly.

sections.title: Worked example: factorise with a negative leading term

prompt.text: Factorise −18x²y + 24xy² completely, leaving a positive first term inside the bracket.

content.text: Find the greatest shared magnitude and variable part.
Choose −6xy so the first bracket term will be positive.

sections.verification_note: Expanding gives −18x²y + 24xy², and 3x and −4y share no numerical or variable factor.

blocks.text: Always multiply the proposed outside factor back through the bracket. Each reconstructed term must match the original coefficient, variables, exponents and sign. This check catches division mistakes immediately and confirms that factorisation has not changed the expression.

Then inspect the bracket for any factor common to every term. If one remains, the original extraction was not greatest. Factorisation is especially useful for revealing a shared structure, solving later equations and rewriting area expressions as products of possible side lengths.

feedback.text: The greatest common factor is 5, so divide both terms by 5 inside the bracket.

blocks.text: For expansion, multiply the outside factor by every term. For factorisation, find the greatest common divisor of the coefficients and the lowest shared power of each variable, divide every term, and place the common factor outside. Re-expand to verify all signs and confirm that no common factor remains inside.
